name: Traceability Matrix - TEP
rows: Governance, risk, internal control and exceptions
The Accountable Authority determines their entity's tolerance for security risks and documents in the security plan.
ICT-enabled projects change NDIA security risk exposure; project governance must align risk acceptance with entity security risk tolerance.
Direct - applies to all NDIA ICT-enabled projects and security assurance decisions.
Projects must identify security risks against NDIA risk tolerance, record residual risk in project assurance artefacts, and escalate exceptions for authorised approval.
Governance, risk, internal control and exceptions
A risk steward (or manager) is identified for each security risk or category of security risk, including shared risks.
Clear risk stewardship is needed so project security risks, including shared risks, are owned through delivery and transition to operations.
Direct - applies to project risk registers, delivery partners and shared platform dependencies.
Each project must assign an accountable owner or steward for each security risk or risk category, including shared risks across business, technology and supplier teams.
Governance, risk, internal control and exceptions
The Accountable Authority considers the impact that their security risk management decisions could potentially have on other entities, and shares information on risks where appropriate.
Technology-enabled change can affect other entities, shared services and government partners; the policy should mandate consultation and risk sharing.
Direct - applies where project decisions affect another entity, provider, scheme partner or shared service.
Projects must assess cross-entity security impacts and share relevant risk information with affected entities or partners through approved governance channels.
Supplier, procurement, contract and digital sourcing governance

The entity is accountable for the management of security risks arising from procuring goods and services and ensures procurement and contract decisions do not expose the entity or the Australian Government to an unacceptable level of risk.
ICT projects frequently procure products and services; procurement decisions must not introduce unacceptable protective security risk.
Direct - applies to project sourcing, procurement strategies, statements of work and contract approvals.
Projects must assess security risks before procurement and contract decisions and must not proceed where the decision creates unacceptable risk to NDIA or the Australian Government.
Supplier, procurement, contract and digital sourcing governance

Procurement, contracts and third-party outsourced arrangements contain proportionate security terms and conditions to ensure service providers, contractors and subcontractors comply with relevant PSPF Requirements.
Security obligations need to be contractually enforceable for suppliers, contractors and subcontractors that deliver ICT-enabled change.
Direct - applies to all supplier engagements, including subcontracted delivery and managed services.
Project procurement documents and contracts must include proportionate PSPF, ISM, privacy, data handling, incident reporting and subcontractor security obligations.
Supplier, procurement, contract and digital sourcing governance
Entity ensures service providers, contractors and subcontractors comply with relevant PSPF Requirements as detailed by the entity.
The TEP policy should require evidence that suppliers comply with NDIA-specified security requirements before and after go-live.
Direct - applies to supplier assurance checkpoints, design reviews, acceptance criteria and BAU handover.
Projects must verify and retain evidence that suppliers, contractors and subcontractors comply with applicable NDIA and PSPF security requirements.
Incident response, data breach, ransomware escalation and lessons learned

Contractual security terms and conditions require service providers to report any actual or suspected security incidents to the entity, and follow reasonable direction from the entity arising from incident investigations.
Supplier incident reporting and cooperation obligations are essential to manage delivery and operational security incidents affecting NDIA systems or data.
Direct - applies to supplier contracts, support models and delivery environments.
Contracts and statements of work must require suppliers to promptly report actual or suspected security incidents and follow reasonable NDIA directions arising from investigations.
Cloud, hosting, outsourced ICT, gateways and shared responsibility
Government entities providing outsourced services provide IRAP assessment reports to the government entities consuming, or looking to consume, their services.
Where a project consumes outsourced government ICT services, IRAP evidence is needed for informed risk-based acceptance.
Conditional - applies where NDIA consumes or assesses outsourced government ICT services.
Projects consuming outsourced government ICT services must obtain and assess current IRAP reports and related assurance artefacts before approval to use the service.
Supplier, procurement, contract and digital sourcing governance

Contract security terms and conditions are monitored and reviewed to ensure the specified security controls, terms and conditions are implemented, operated and maintained by the contracted provider, including any subcontractors, over the life of a contract.
Security terms are ineffective unless monitored; project governance must establish assurance that continues into contract management.
Direct - applies to project delivery, contract management planning and transition to operations.
Ongoing supplier assurance and contract management
Projects must define how contracted security controls, terms and subcontractor obligations will be monitored, reviewed and handed over for ongoing contract management.
Supplier, procurement, contract and digital sourcing governance
Contractual terms and conditions include appropriate security arrangements for the completion or termination of the contract.
Exit, termination and transition activities can expose NDIA data, credentials and assets if not designed up front.
Direct - applies to supplier contracts, transition-out plans and decommissioning activities.
Contracts must include secure completion or termination arrangements, including access removal, return or destruction of information, asset return and transition assurance.
Supplier, procurement, contract and digital sourcing governance
Procurement and contract decisions consider the security risks before engaging providers operating under foreign ownership, control or influence.
Technology providers may present foreign ownership, control or influence risks that should be considered before procurement or continued use.
Direct - applies to technology procurement, maintenance, managed services and major supplier changes.
Projects must consider foreign ownership, control or influence risks for technology assets and providers, document the assessment, and escalate material risks for approval.
Supplier, procurement, contract and digital sourcing governance
Security risks arising from contractual arrangements for the provision of goods and services are managed, reassessed and adjusted over the life of a contract.
Supplier risk changes over the life of a project and contract; reassessment must be built into project stage gates and material change controls.
Direct - applies throughout project delivery and supplier contract lifecycle.
Projects must reassess and adjust supplier security risks at stage gates, contract variations, material changes, go-live and transition to operations.
Supplier, procurement, contract and digital sourcing governance
Secure and verifiable third-party vendors, providers, partners and associated services are used unless business operations require use, and the residual risks are managed and approved by the CISO.
Projects should use secure, approved and verifiable third parties or obtain explicit acceptance of residual risk.
Direct - applies to vendor selection, SaaS, cloud, integration partners and delivery tooling.
Projects must use secure and verifiable third-party vendors and services unless a business need is approved and residual risks are accepted by the CISO or delegate.
Governance, risk, internal control and exceptions

Where exceptional circumstances prevent or affect an entity's capability to implement a PSPF requirement or standard, the Accountable Authority may vary application, for a limited period of time, consistent with the entity's risk tolerance.
Projects may seek time-limited variations where delivery constraints prevent full compliance; the policy must govern such exceptions.
Conditional - applies when exceptional circumstances prevent or affect PSPF implementation in a project.
Any project seeking a variation from a PSPF requirement must document exceptional circumstances, time limits, compensating controls and alignment with NDIA risk tolerance.
Governance, risk, internal control and exceptions
Decisions to vary implementation of a PSPF requirement or standard due to exceptional circumstances are documented in the entity's security plan.
Approved variations must be traceable in security planning and assurance records so residual risk remains visible.
Conditional - applies where a project variation, waiver or temporary exception is approved.
Approved PSPF variations must be recorded in the relevant security plan, project risk register and assurance decision record, with owner, expiry and review date.
Governance, risk, internal control and exceptions
Decisions to implement an alternative mitigation measure that meets or exceeds a PSPF requirement or standard are reviewed and reported annually.
Alternative controls chosen by projects need periodic review and reporting to confirm they continue to meet or exceed the mandatory requirement.
Conditional - applies where projects use compensating or alternative mitigation measures.
Projects using alternative mitigation measures must demonstrate equivalence or uplift against the PSPF requirement and ensure review and reporting obligations are assigned.
Information classification, caveats, external sharing and DATA Scheme controls

The value, importance or sensitivity of official information is assessed by the originator by considering the potential damage to the government, the national interest, organisations or individuals that would arise if the information's confidentiality were compromised.
ICT projects create, migrate and integrate official information; security classification and sensitivity assessment must be performed early.
Direct - applies to project information, data sets, records, environments and system design.
Projects must assess the value, importance and sensitivity of information and data holdings during discovery and maintain this assessment through design and change control.
Information classification, caveats, external sharing and DATA Scheme controls
The minimum protections and handling requirements are applied to protect OFFICIAL and security classified information.
Project environments and collaboration spaces must protect OFFICIAL and classified information according to minimum handling requirements.
Direct - applies to project documentation, data migration, testing, environments and collaboration tooling.
Projects must apply minimum protections and handling requirements for OFFICIAL, OFFICIAL: Sensitive and security classified information in all project stores and environments.
Information classification, caveats, external sharing and DATA Scheme controls
The Australian Government Security Caveat Standard and special handling requirements imposed by the controlling authority are applied to protect security caveated information.
If project information is security caveated, controls must enforce the caveat and any special handling obligations.
Conditional - applies where caveated information or special handling information is used, stored or shared.
Projects handling caveated information must implement the required caveat markings, access restrictions, transfer controls and special handling requirements before use.
Information classification, caveats, external sharing and DATA Scheme controls

The Australian Government Email Protective Marking Standard is applied to protect OFFICIAL and security classified information exchanged by email in and between Australian Government entities, including other authorised parties.
Project teams exchange information by email; protective markings are required to preserve handling requirements in communications.
Direct - applies to project emails containing official, sensitive or classified information.
Project communications must apply Australian Government email protective markings when exchanging OFFICIAL or security classified information with NDIA or authorised parties.
Records, FOI readiness, metadata, retention, disposal and decommissioning

The Australian Government Recordkeeping Metadata Standard's 'Security Classification' property (and where relevant, the 'Security Caveat' property) is applied to protectively mark information on technology systems that store, process or communicate security classified information.
Systems delivered by ICT projects may need metadata fields that preserve classification and caveat attributes for records and access control.
Conditional - applies where a system stores, processes or communicates security classified information.
Projects must include recordkeeping metadata requirements for security classification and caveat properties where systems store, process or communicate classified information.
Records, FOI readiness, metadata, retention, disposal and decommissioning
Apply the Australian Government Recordkeeping Metadata Standard's 'Rights' property where the entity wishes to categorise information content by the type of restrictions on access.
Access restrictions need to be represented in system metadata where information content is categorised by rights or restrictions.
Conditional - applies where project systems use rights metadata or restriction categories to manage access.
Where access restrictions are used, projects must support the Rights metadata property or an approved equivalent in system requirements and information architecture.
Information classification, caveats, external sharing and DATA Scheme controls
Entity implements operational controls for its information holdings that are proportional to their value, importance and sensitivity.
ICT-enabled projects affect NDIA information holdings; operational controls must match the value and sensitivity of those holdings.
Direct - applies to data architecture, operational readiness, controls design and handover.
Projects must identify affected information holdings and implement operational controls proportionate to their value, importance, sensitivity and business impact.
Records, FOI readiness, metadata, retention, disposal and decommissioning

OFFICIAL and security classified information is disposed of securely in accordance with the Minimum Protections and Handling Requirements, ISM, the Records Authorities, a Normal Administrative Practice and the Archives Act 1983.
Projects often migrate, archive or decommission information; secure disposal must be designed into project closure and system retirement.
Direct - applies to data migration, test data, media, decommissioning and records disposal activities.
Projects must plan and execute secure disposal of official information, assets and media in accordance with minimum handling requirements, the ISM and records obligations.
Records, FOI readiness, metadata, retention, disposal and decommissioning

Security classified information is appropriately destroyed in accordance with the Minimum Protections and Handling Requirements when it has passed the minimum retention requirements or reaches authorised destruction dates.
Classified information requires specific destruction controls once retention obligations are met or authorised destruction dates are reached.
Conditional - applies where project activities handle or dispose of security classified information.
Projects disposing of security classified information must confirm retention authority and use approved destruction methods before disposal or decommissioning is completed.
Information classification, caveats, external sharing and DATA Scheme controls

Access to security classified information or resources is only provided to people outside the entity with the appropriate security clearance (where required) and a need-to-know, and is transferred in accordance with the Minimum Protections and Handling Requirements.
ICT projects often provide external parties access to systems and data; clearance, need-to-know and transfer controls must be mandated.
Direct - applies to suppliers, consultants, delivery partners and external users with access to NDIA information or systems.
Projects must only grant external access to information or resources where need-to-know, clearance where required, and approved transfer controls are confirmed.
Information classification, caveats, external sharing and DATA Scheme controls
The Memorandum of Understanding between the Commonwealth, States and Territories is applied when sharing information with state and territory government agencies.
Some NDIA projects may share information with state or territory agencies; the applicable government MOU must be considered.
Conditional - applies where a project shares information with state or territory government agencies.
Information sharing with state and territory agencies
Projects sharing information with state or territory agencies must confirm the applicable MOU or arrangement and implement required handling, access and transfer controls.
Information classification, caveats, external sharing and DATA Scheme controls
An agreement or arrangement is in place before security classified information or resources are disclosed or shared with a person or organisation outside of government.
Sharing classified information with external non-government parties requires a formal agreement before disclosure.
Conditional - applies where security classified information is disclosed to vendors, partners or other non-government organisations.
Projects must not disclose or share security classified information or resources outside government unless an approved agreement or arrangement is in place.
Information classification, caveats, external sharing and DATA Scheme controls
Provisions are met concerning the security of people, information and resources contained in international agreements and arrangements to which Australia is a party.
International arrangements can impose security obligations that must be reflected in project design and delivery decisions.
Conditional - applies where project scope includes international partners, offshore services or cross-border information sharing.
International information sharing and offshore access
Projects with international information sharing or offshore access must identify relevant international agreements and implement required security provisions before approval.
Information classification, caveats, external sharing and DATA Scheme controls

Australian Government security classified information or resources shared with a foreign entity is protected by an explicit legislative provision, international agreement or international arrangement.
Classified Australian Government information cannot be shared with foreign entities without a valid legal or agreement basis.
Conditional - applies where a project proposes sharing classified information or resources with a foreign entity.
Projects must not share security classified information or resources with a foreign entity unless authorised by legislation, an international agreement or an arrangement.
Information classification, caveats, external sharing and DATA Scheme controls

Australian Government security classified information or resources bearing the AUSTEO caveat is never shared with a person who is not an Australian citizen, even when an international agreement or arrangement is in place, unless an exemption is granted.
AUSTEO material has strict citizenship restrictions that project access models and collaboration spaces must enforce.
Conditional - applies only where AUSTEO caveated information or resources are in scope.
Projects must prevent access to AUSTEO information by non-Australian citizens unless a valid exemption is granted and recorded.
Information classification, caveats, external sharing and DATA Scheme controls
Australian Government security classified information or resources bearing the AGAO caveat is not shared with a person who is not an Australian citizen, except as specified.
AGAO caveated material also requires specific citizenship and access restrictions to be enforced by project controls.
Conditional - applies only where AGAO caveated information or resources are in scope.
Projects must enforce AGAO caveat restrictions, including citizenship and approved access limitations, in identity, access and information-sharing designs.
Information classification, caveats, external sharing and DATA Scheme controls

Where an international agreement or arrangement is in place, security classified foreign entity information or resources are safeguarded in accordance with the provisions set out in the agreement or arrangement.
Foreign entity information received under an agreement must be protected according to that agreement within project systems and processes.
Conditional - applies where foreign entity information or resources are stored, processed or communicated.
Projects must safeguard foreign entity classified information or resources in accordance with the relevant agreement or arrangement and approved handling controls.
Information classification, caveats, external sharing and DATA Scheme controls

Australian Government security classified information or resources shared with a foreign non-government stakeholder is protected by an explicit legislative provision, international agreement or international arrangement.
Sharing Australian Government classified information with foreign non-government stakeholders must be legally enabled and controlled.
Conditional - applies where a project proposes disclosure to foreign non-government stakeholders.
Projects must not share classified Australian Government information or resources with foreign non-government stakeholders unless authorised by legislation or an approved agreement.
Secure-by-design lifecycle, system definition, change control and authorisation
The Australian Signals Directorate's Information Security Manual cyber security principles are applied during all stages of the lifecycle of each system.
The TEP policy is a delivery framework for ICT-enabled change and must embed ISM principles across the system lifecycle.
Direct - applies to all new and changed NDIA technology systems and services.
Projects must apply ASD ISM cyber security principles from discovery through design, build, test, authorisation, release, operation and decommissioning.
Secure-by-design lifecycle, system definition, change control and authorisation
The Australian Signals Directorate's Information Security Manual controls and cyber security guidelines are applied on a risk-based approach.
Risk-based ISM control selection and assurance are core to project architecture and security obligations.
Direct - applies to solution architecture, control design, assurance and security acceptance.
Projects must select, implement and assess ISM controls on a risk-based approach and maintain evidence for architecture, security and assurance reviews.
Secure-by-design lifecycle, system definition, change control and authorisation

The Authorising Officer authorises each technology system to operate based on the acceptance of the residual security risks associated with its operation before that system processes, stores or communicates government information or data.
Systems should not process NDIA or government information until residual security risk is authorised by the appropriate officer.
Direct - applies before go-live, pilot use, production data use or operational release.
Authority to operate and residual risk acceptance
Projects must obtain authorisation to operate from the Authorising Officer before a technology system processes, stores or communicates government information or data.
Secure-by-design lifecycle, system definition, change control and authorisation
Decisions to authorise (or reauthorise) a new technology system or make changes to an existing technology system are based on the ISM's risk-based approach to cyber security.
Major project changes require authorisation decisions based on updated cyber risk and control assurance.
Direct - applies to new systems and material changes to existing systems.
Security authorisation for new systems and changes
Projects must base authorisation and reauthorisation decisions for new systems or changes on the ISM risk-based approach and documented residual risk.
Secure-by-design lifecycle, system definition, change control and authorisation
The technology system is authorised to the highest security classification of the information and data it will process, store or communicate.
System authorisation must reflect the highest classification of information the system will handle.
Direct - applies to classification, architecture, environment, hosting and authorisation decisions.
Projects must determine the highest classification of information or data in scope and ensure the system is authorised and protected to that level.
Secure-by-design lifecycle, system definition, change control and authorisation

A register of the entity's authorised technology systems is developed, implemented and maintained, and includes the name and position of the Authorising Officer, system owner, date of authorisation, and any decisions to accept residual security risks.
Project outputs must update NDIA system registers so authorised systems, owners and accepted residual risks remain visible.
Direct - applies to go-live readiness, operational handover and system register maintenance.
Projects must update the authorised technology systems register with system owner, Authorising Officer, authorisation date and accepted residual security risks.
Secure-by-design lifecycle, system definition, change control and authorisation

Each technology system's suitability to be authorised to operate is reassessed when it undergoes significant functionality or architectural change, or where the system's security environment has changed considerably.
Significant project functionality, architecture or threat changes can invalidate prior authorisation and require reassessment.
Direct - applies to change impact assessment and release governance.
Projects must trigger security reassessment where functionality, architecture, environment or threat context changes materially before release or continued operation.
Secure-by-design lifecycle, system definition, change control and authorisation
The TikTok application is prevented from being installed, and existing instances are removed, on government devices, unless a legitimate business reason exists.
Technology-enabled projects may introduce devices, apps or web services; the policy should require compliance with prohibited technology directions.
Direct - applies to project devices, managed endpoints, delivery tooling and application whitelisting.
Projects must prevent installation or use of prohibited applications such as TikTok on government devices unless an approved business exception exists.
Secure-by-design lifecycle, system definition, change control and authorisation
The CSO or CISO approves any legitimate business reason for the use of the TikTok application on government devices and ensures specified mitigations are in place.
Any exception to a prohibited technology requirement needs senior security approval and mitigations.
Conditional - applies only where a legitimate business reason for TikTok use is proposed.
Projects proposing use of TikTok on government devices must obtain CSO or CISO approval and implement specified mitigations before use.
Secure-by-design lifecycle, system definition, change control and authorisation
The Australian Signals Directorate's temporary mitigations for legacy IT are applied to manage legacy information technology that cannot yet be replaced.
Many ICT change projects depend on legacy IT; temporary mitigations must be required until replacement or remediation is completed.
Conditional - applies where project scope involves legacy, unsupported or hard-to-replace technology.
Legacy technology remediation and temporary mitigations
Projects involving legacy IT must apply ASD temporary mitigations, document residual risks and include remediation or replacement actions in delivery plans.
Physical security, facilities, security zones and technology asset protection
Technology assets and their components, classified as SECRET or below are stored in the appropriate Security Zone based on their aggregated security classification or business impact level.
Physical storage protections for classified technology assets are dependencies for solution design, deployment and operations.
Conditional - applies where project assets or components are classified SECRET or below or have aggregated impact.
Projects must confirm classified technology assets and components are stored in an appropriate Security Zone based on classification aggregation or business impact level.
Physical security, facilities, security zones and technology asset protection
Technology assets and their components classified as TOP SECRET are stored in suitable SCEC-endorsed racks or compartments within an accredited Security Zone Five area.
TOP SECRET technology assets have specialised physical storage controls that must be identified early if in scope.
Conditional - rare; applies only to TOP SECRET technology assets or components.
Projects involving TOP SECRET technology assets must use suitable SCEC-endorsed racks or compartments within an accredited Security Zone Five area.
Physical security, facilities, security zones and technology asset protection

Outsourced facilities that house technology assets and their components with a catastrophic business impact level are certified by ASIO T4 physical security and accredited by ASD before they are used operationally.
Catastrophic business impact technology assets require certified and accredited outsourced facilities before operational use.
Conditional - applies where outsourced facilities house catastrophic business impact technology assets.
Outsourced facility certification for high-impact assets
Projects must verify outsourced facilities housing catastrophic business impact technology assets are ASIO T4 certified and ASD accredited before operational use.
Records, FOI readiness, metadata, retention, disposal and decommissioning
Technology assets are disposed of securely in accordance with the Information Security Manual.
Project decommissioning, asset refresh and disposal activities must prevent data or configuration exposure.
Direct - applies to decommissioning, asset replacement, media sanitisation and disposal.
Projects must securely dispose of technology assets and components in accordance with the ISM and record disposal evidence before closure.
Cyber strategy, Essential Eight, control baseline and vulnerability management

A cyber security strategy and uplift plan is developed, implemented and maintained to manage the entity's cyber security risks in accordance with the ISM and the Guiding Principles to Embed a Zero Trust Culture.
Technology-enabled projects are a key mechanism for delivering cyber uplift and embedding zero trust-aligned controls.
Direct - applies to project alignment with NDIA cyber strategy, security roadmap and uplift priorities.
Cyber strategy and zero trust alignment
Projects must align designs, delivery plans and assurance evidence with the NDIA cyber security strategy, uplift plan and zero trust-aligned principles.
Cyber strategy, Essential Eight, control baseline and vulnerability management
Patch applications mitigation strategy is implemented to Maturity Level Two under ASD's Essential Eight Maturity Model.
Application patching must be designed into systems and operational handover to meet mandated Essential Eight maturity.
Direct - applies to applications introduced, configured, changed or supported by projects.
Projects must define, implement and hand over application patching controls that meet Essential Eight Maturity Level Two before production release.
Cyber strategy, Essential Eight, control baseline and vulnerability management
Patch operating systems mitigation strategy is implemented to Maturity Level Two under ASD's Essential Eight Maturity Model.
Operating system patching must be built into environments, devices and support arrangements delivered by projects.
Direct - applies to servers, endpoints, appliances and operating environments in project scope.
Projects must define, implement and hand over operating system patching controls that meet Essential Eight Maturity Level Two before production release.
Cyber strategy, Essential Eight, control baseline and vulnerability management
Multi-factor authentication mitigation strategy is implemented to Maturity Level Two under ASD's Essential Eight Maturity Model.
MFA is a baseline access control for ICT-enabled change and must be designed into identity and access management.
Direct - applies to user, privileged, remote, cloud and administrative access patterns.
Projects must implement multi-factor authentication controls that meet Essential Eight Maturity Level Two for applicable users and access paths.
Cyber strategy, Essential Eight, control baseline and vulnerability management
Restrict administrative privileges mitigation strategy is implemented to Maturity Level Two under ASD's Essential Eight Maturity Model.
Restricting administrative privileges is required to reduce compromise risk in new and changed systems.
Direct - applies to privileged accounts, administration tools, support models and service providers.
Projects must minimise, segregate, monitor and periodically review administrative privileges in line with Essential Eight Maturity Level Two.
Cyber strategy, Essential Eight, control baseline and vulnerability management
Application control mitigation strategy is implemented to Maturity Level Two under ASD's Essential Eight Maturity Model.
Application control reduces execution of unauthorised code and must be considered in endpoint and server designs.
Direct - applies to project-managed endpoints, servers and application execution environments.
Projects must implement application control for applicable platforms and workloads to meet Essential Eight Maturity Level Two.
Cyber strategy, Essential Eight, control baseline and vulnerability management
Restrict Microsoft Office macros mitigation strategy is implemented to Maturity Level Two under ASD's Essential Eight Maturity Model.
Macro controls are needed where project solutions use Microsoft Office or related document workflows.
Direct - applies where Office documents, collaboration platforms or macro-enabled workflows are in scope.
Essential Eight - restrict Microsoft Office macros
Projects must restrict Microsoft Office macros in accordance with Essential Eight Maturity Level Two and avoid introducing macro-dependent business processes unless approved.
Cyber strategy, Essential Eight, control baseline and vulnerability management
User application hardening mitigation strategy is implemented to Maturity Level Two under ASD's Essential Eight Maturity Model.
User application hardening must be reflected in desktop, browser and application configuration delivered or affected by projects.
Direct - applies to end-user computing, browser, PDF, web and collaboration components in scope.
Projects must implement user application hardening controls that meet Essential Eight Maturity Level Two before production deployment.
Cyber strategy, Essential Eight, control baseline and vulnerability management
Regular back-ups mitigation strategy is implemented to Maturity Level Two under ASD's Essential Eight Maturity Model.
Backups and restoration arrangements are essential for resilience of systems delivered or changed by projects.
Direct - applies to data stores, applications, platforms and operational recovery requirements.
Projects must design, implement, test and hand over backup and restoration controls that meet Essential Eight Maturity Level Two.
Cyber strategy, Essential Eight, control baseline and vulnerability management

The remaining mitigation strategies from the Strategies to Mitigate Cyber Security Incidents are considered and, where required, implemented to achieve an acceptable level of residual risk for their entity.
Beyond the Essential Eight, projects may need additional mitigations to achieve acceptable residual risk for the threat environment.
Direct - applies through risk assessment and security control selection for all projects.
Projects must consider ASD Strategies to Mitigate Cyber Security Incidents and implement additional controls where required to achieve acceptable residual risk.
Cyber strategy, Essential Eight, control baseline and vulnerability management
A Protective Domain Name System service or other security mechanisms is used to prevent connections to and from known malicious endpoints.
Projects introducing or changing internet-connected systems must ensure malicious endpoint protections are included in network and gateway design.
Direct - applies to internet-connected systems, services, endpoints and cloud workloads.
Protective DNS and malicious endpoint controls
Projects must ensure internet-connected systems use Protective DNS or other approved security mechanisms to prevent connections to and from known malicious endpoints.
Cloud, hosting, outsourced ICT, gateways and shared responsibility
Cloud Service Providers that have completed an IRAP assessment against the latest version of ASD's ISM within the previous 24 months are used.
Cloud sourcing decisions in ICT projects require current IRAP evidence against the latest ISM.
Conditional - applies where project scope includes Cloud Service Providers or cloud-hosted services.
Projects must use Cloud Service Providers with an IRAP assessment against the latest ASD ISM completed within the previous 24 months.
Cloud, hosting, outsourced ICT, gateways and shared responsibility
Entities consider IRAP assessment recommendations and findings, and implement on a risk-based approach.
IRAP reports produce findings that must be evaluated and treated rather than simply collected.
Conditional - applies where IRAP-assessed services, cloud platforms or managed services are used.
Projects must review IRAP recommendations and findings, record risk treatments, and ensure residual risks are accepted through project security governance.
Cloud, hosting, outsourced ICT, gateways and shared responsibility

Security classified or systems of government significance information and data is securely hosted using a Cloud Service Provider and Data Centre Provider that has been certified against the Australian Government Hosting Certification Framework.
Sensitive hosting choices are core architecture decisions for classified or systems of government significance information.
Conditional - applies where classified or systems of government significance information is hosted or processed.
Projects must host classified or systems of government significance information using certified Cloud Service Providers and Data Centre Providers under the Hosting Certification Framework.
Cloud, hosting, outsourced ICT, gateways and shared responsibility
The Data Centre Facilities Supplies Panel is used when procuring certified data centre space and services.
Projects procuring certified data centre services must use the appropriate whole-of-government arrangement.
Conditional - applies where project scope includes procurement of certified data centre space or services.
Projects procuring certified data centre space or services must use the Data Centre Facilities Supplies Panel or approved whole-of-government procurement pathway.
Cloud, hosting, outsourced ICT, gateways and shared responsibility
Internet-connected technology systems, and the data they process, store or communicate, are protected by a gateway in accordance with the ISM and the Gateways Policy.
Internet-connected systems require gateway protections as part of architecture and security assurance.
Direct - applies to internet-connected systems and data flows delivered or changed by projects.
Projects must protect internet-connected technology systems and the data they process, store or communicate using approved gateway controls aligned to the ISM and Gateways Policy.
Cloud, hosting, outsourced ICT, gateways and shared responsibility
Gateways or Secure Service Edges that have completed an IRAP assessment (or ASD assessment for TOP SECRET gateways) against the latest version of ASD's ISM within the previous 24 months are used.
Gateway and Security Service Edge services require current independent assurance before use for protected data flows.
Conditional - applies where projects introduce or materially change gateways or Secure Service Edge services.
Gateway and Secure Service Edge assurance
Projects must use gateways or Secure Service Edge services with a current IRAP assessment, or ASD assessment for TOP SECRET gateways, before production use.
Cyber strategy, Essential Eight, control baseline and vulnerability management
A vulnerability disclosure program and supporting processes and procedures are established to receive, verify, resolve and report on vulnerabilities disclosed by both internal and external sources.
Vulnerability disclosure must be integrated with new or changed digital services so vulnerabilities are received, verified and remediated.
Direct - applies to public-facing, internet-connected or materially changed digital services.
Projects must integrate delivered systems with NDIA vulnerability disclosure, triage, remediation and reporting processes before go-live.
Physical security, facilities, security zones and technology asset protection
Protective security is integrated in the process of planning, selecting, designing and modifying entity facilities for the protection of people, information and resources.
ICT projects can change facilities, contact centres, secure rooms or data centre spaces; protective security must be considered during planning and design.
Conditional interface - applies when a project creates, modifies or depends on a facility or secure work area.
Physical security dependencies for ICT projects
Projects affecting facilities must engage protective security and facilities stakeholders early to integrate security requirements into planning, design and modification decisions.
Physical security, facilities, security zones and technology asset protection
A facility security plan is developed for new facilities, facilities under construction or major refurbishments of existing facilities.
Major facility changes supporting ICT delivery may require a facility security plan before construction or refurbishment.
Conditional interface - applies to new facilities, construction or major refurbishment in project scope.
Projects involving new facilities or major refurbishments must confirm whether a facility security plan is required and include it in project deliverables.
Physical security, facilities, security zones and technology asset protection
Decisions on entity facility locations are informed by considering the site selection factors for Australian Government facilities.
Site location can affect resilience, access, security zoning and protection of ICT assets and personnel.

The Act includes protections for disclosers and provisions relating to reprisal action.
Project delivery pressure can create retaliation or suppression risks if concerns are raised.
Applies to NDIA project environments, including mixed teams of officials and contractors.
Project leaders must prevent and escalate any suspected reprisal, victimisation or adverse action connected with a disclosure or suspected disclosure.

PID Act - principal officer, authorised officer and supervisor obligations
The Act sets obligations for principal officers, authorised officers, supervisors and public officials in handling disclosures.
Project managers and supervisors need to know when a concern may be a PID and should not investigate outside the statutory process.
Applies to NDIA supervisors, managers and project governance participants.
Project managers must promptly refer potential public interest disclosures to authorised NDIA channels and must not dismiss, reclassify or investigate them without appropriate advice.

The Ombudsman guidance notes that the PID framework can apply to contracted service providers and supports agency procedures, training and culture.
Vendor delivery is in scope and supplier personnel may be the first to identify wrongdoing.
Applies to NDIA contracts and supplier onboarding where Commonwealth contracted service provider provisions apply.
Contracts and onboarding materials should explain PID rights and obligations for relevant supplier personnel and preserve access to NDIA disclosure pathways.

PGPA Act s16 and Commonwealth Risk Management Policy
The CRMP supports the PGPA Act requirement to establish appropriate risk oversight, management and internal controls.
Project risk management is an explicit scope area and must connect to enterprise risk, not sit only in delivery logs.
PGPA s16 directly applies to NDIA. CRMP is directly binding on NCEs and should be applied by NDIA where adopted or as better practice.
Project risk management must align with NDIA enterprise risk arrangements, including risk appetite, ownership, treatment, escalation and reporting.

Commonwealth Risk Management Policy - risk embedded in decision-making
The policy promotes risk management as part of governance, planning, delivery and decision-making.
Gateway decisions should be based on risk evidence and options, not only schedule and budget.
Relevant to all NDIA technology-enabled projects and portfolio decisions.
Gate packs must present current delivery, security, privacy, fraud, procurement, dependency, benefit and operational risks, including residual risk after controls.

Commonwealth Risk Management Policy - shared and emerging risks
The policy encourages entities to manage risks that cut across organisational boundaries and evolve over time.
ICT projects create cross-portfolio dependencies and emerging risks in cyber, data, suppliers and operations.
Applies to NDIA portfolio reporting and dependency management.
Projects must identify shared risks and dependencies with other NDIA initiatives, whole-of-government services and suppliers, and escalate conflicts through portfolio governance.

Cyber Security Act 2024 and Cyber Security (Ransomware Payment Reporting) Rules 2025
Cyber Security Act Part 2 - security standards for smart devices
The Act provides for mandatory security standards for relevant connectable products, supported by Rules.
Technology projects may procure smart devices, sensors, hardware, kiosks, assistive or connected products that connect to networks or services.
Applies if NDIA procures, supplies, pilots or integrates products that fall within the relevant connectable product regime or requires supplier compliance evidence.
Projects procuring or integrating connected devices must assess whether smart device security standards apply and require supplier statements of compliance where relevant.

Cyber Security Act 2024 and Cyber Security (Ransomware Payment Reporting) Rules 2026
Cyber Security Act Part 3 and Rules - ransomware payment reporting
The Act and Rules establish reporting obligations for ransomware or cyber extortion payments for covered entities and prescribed information.
Project delivery and operations handover should include incident escalation and ransomware decision controls.
Applicability to NDIA must be confirmed by legal/security advice for the specific incident and entity context; suppliers may have direct obligations.
Projects must ensure cyber incident and ransomware escalation paths are defined for delivery, testing, cutover, hypercare and supplier-operated environments.

Cyber Security Act 2024 and Cyber Security (Ransomware Payment Reporting) Rules 2027
Cyber Security Act Part 4 - significant cyber security incident coordination and limited use
Impacted entities may voluntarily provide information to the National Cyber Security Coordinator, with limited-use protections in the Act.
Major projects and service transitions need clear whole-of-government cyber incident coordination pathways.
Relevant to NDIA security incident response and project transition arrangements, especially for significant incidents.
Project security and operations handover must identify when significant cyber incidents are escalated to NDIA security leadership and whole-of-government coordination channels.

Cyber Security Act 2024 and Cyber Security (Ransomware Payment Reporting) Rules 2028
Cyber Security Act Part 5 - Cyber Incident Review Board
The Act establishes a Cyber Incident Review Board to conduct no-fault post-incident reviews of significant cyber incidents.
Post-implementation review and lessons learned must include cyber incident lessons where applicable.
Relevant where NDIA or its suppliers are involved in a significant cyber incident that may be reviewed.
Projects and operations teams must preserve evidence and cooperate with authorised post-incident reviews, while tracking lessons learned into remediation and future project controls.
